Maps and boundaries

Source: vignettes/articles/maps.Rmd
maps.Rmd
library(phwstyle)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)

All data on this page is made up. The boundaries are real, and they download the first time you use a level.

Draw a map with phw_map()

phw_map() joins your data to Welsh boundaries and draws a styled map in one call. Give it your data, the column of area codes (by), the column to colour by (fill) and the boundary level. Areas with no row in your data are grey. The boundary attribution becomes the caption unless you set your own with labs().

codes <- phw_boundaries("health_board")
hb <- tibble(code = codes$code, rate = round(runif(nrow(codes), 20, 80), 1))

Continuous fills

A numeric fill gets a continuous scale in the "blues" palette. Change it with palette.

phw_map(hb, by = code, fill = rate, level = "health_board") +
  labs(fill = "Rate per\n100,000", title = "Rate by health board")

Binned fills

Give bins a set of breaks, or a single number of bins, to colour by band. The legend also shows the lowest and highest values, rounded out to tidy numbers, so both ends of your data are covered.

phw_map(hb, by = code, fill = rate, level = "health_board", bins = c(40, 50, 60, 70)) +
  labs(fill = "Rate per\n100,000", title = "Rate by health board")

Groups, with a colour key

A text or factor column gives one colour per group. Give key the name of a colour key and each group keeps its colour in every map, chart and table that uses it. See colour keys.

hb$band <- rep_len(c("Group A", "Group B", "Group C"), nrow(hb))
phw_map(hb, by = code, fill = band, level = "health_board", key = "map_groups") +
  labs(fill = NULL, title = "Health boards by group")

Labels

label prints text on each area. Give it a column, or an expression built from the columns of your data and the boundary name. When ggrepel is installed, labels on small areas are moved apart so they stay readable.

la_codes <- phw_boundaries("local_authority")
la <- tibble(code = la_codes$code, rate = round(runif(nrow(la_codes), 20, 80), 1))
phw_map(la, by = code, fill = rate, level = "local_authority",
        label = paste(name, rate), bins = c(40, 50, 60, 70)) +
  labs(fill = "Rate", title = "Rate by local authority")

One map per period

phw_map() takes one row per area and period. Add facet_wrap() to draw one map for each period, on the same scale.

hb_years <- tidyr::expand_grid(code = codes$code, year = c(2024, 2025)) |>
  mutate(rate = round(runif(n(), 20, 80), 1))
phw_map(hb_years, by = code, fill = rate, level = "health_board", bins = c(40, 50, 60, 70)) +
  facet_wrap(vars(year)) +
  labs(fill = "Rate", title = "Rate by health board")

Level of detail

detail sets how finely the outlines are drawn. The default "generalised" suits most maps. "super" and "ultra" give smaller files, and "full" is clipped to the coastline.

phw_map(la, by = code, fill = rate, level = "local_authority", detail = "ultra") +
  labs(fill = "Rate", title = "ultra")

phw_map(la, by = code, fill = rate, level = "local_authority", detail = "full") +
  labs(fill = "Rate", title = "full")

Build your own map

phw_boundaries() returns an sf data frame with code, name, name_cy (where the source has Welsh names) and the geometry. Join your own data on code, then draw it with geom_sf(). scale_fill_phw_b() gives a binned scale and theme_phw_map() removes the axes and grid.

hb_sf <- phw_boundaries("health_board") |>
  left_join(hb, by = "code")

ggplot(hb_sf) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = rate), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_phw_b(name = "Rate per\n100,000") +
  theme_phw_map() +
  labs(title = "Rate by health board",
       caption = paste(strwrap(attr(hb_sf, "attribution"), 60), collapse = "\n"))

Levels

phw_boundary_levels() lists every level and the release used for it. GP clusters, LSOAs and the other levels work like the examples above.

phw_boundary_levels()
#>                       level                                          label
#> 1                   country                                Country (Wales)
#> 2              health_board                            Local health boards
#> 3           local_authority                              Local authorities
#> 4                gp_cluster                     GP (primary care) clusters
#> 5       senedd_constituency                          Senedd constituencies
#> 6  westminster_constituency                   UK Parliament constituencies
#> 7            electoral_ward                                Electoral wards
#> 8                 community Communities (community and town council areas)
#> 9                      msoa         Middle layer super output areas (2021)
#> 10                     lsoa          Lower layer super output areas (2021)
#> 11              output_area                            Output areas (2021)
#> 12              fire_rescue                    Fire and rescue authorities
#> 13             police_force                             Police force areas
#>          source release                          detail
#> 1           ons    2025 full, generalised, super, ultra
#> 2           ons    2023        full, generalised, ultra
#> 3           ons    2026 full, generalised, super, ultra
#> 4  datamapwales    2024                            full
#> 5           ons    2026        full, generalised, super
#> 6           ons    2024 full, generalised, super, ultra
#> 7           ons    2026        full, generalised, super
#> 8  datamapwales    2022                            full
#> 9  datamapwales    2021                     full, super
#> 10 datamapwales    2021                     full, super
#> 11          ons    2021                     generalised
#> 12          ons    2024        full, generalised, ultra
#> 13          ons    2024        full, generalised, ultra
gp <- phw_boundaries("gp_cluster")
ggplot(gp) +
  geom_sf(fill = phw_colours[["light_teal"]], colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  theme_phw_map() +
  labs(title = paste(nrow(gp), "GP clusters"))

Interactive maps

phw_leaflet() starts a leaflet map on Wales, with a light grey base map. phw_leaflet_polygons() adds your areas. It takes the same fill, bins and key as phw_map(), plus label and popup for what appears on hover and click. Ask for longitude and latitude with crs = 4326.

hb_ll <- phw_boundaries("health_board", crs = 4326) |>
  left_join(hb, by = "code")
phw_leaflet() |>
  phw_leaflet_polygons(hb_ll, fill = rate, bins = 4, label = name, legend_title = "Rate")

phw_leaflet_palette() makes the colour function that phw_leaflet_polygons() uses. Use it when you add layers with leaflet itself and want the same colours.

pal <- phw_leaflet_palette("blues", domain = hb_ll$rate, type = "bin", bins = 4)
phw_leaflet() |>
  leaflet::addPolygons(data = hb_ll, fillColor = ~pal(rate), fillOpacity = 0.8,
                       weight = 1, color = "#FFFFFF", label = ~name) |>
  leaflet::addLegend(pal = pal, values = hb_ll$rate, title = "Rate")

For more interactive output, see the interactive article. For finished examples, see the gallery.

Keeping boundaries up to date

When ONS or the Welsh Government publish new boundaries, a new version of phwstyle points to them. After updating phwstyle, refresh your cached copies:

phw_boundaries("electoral_ward", refresh = TRUE)
phw_boundaries_cache(clear = TRUE)   # or clear everything

You don’t have to update phwstyle for your maps to keep working:

  • Boundaries you have already downloaded are read from your cache, so they don’t change and don’t need a connection.
  • Where a geography has two sources, the second is used if the first can’t be reached.
  • If a publisher withdraws a layer that your version of phwstyle lists, phw_boundaries() fetches the current list of layers from the phwstyle repository on GitHub and uses that. The list is checked against both publishers every week. Set options(phwstyle.boundary_update = FALSE) if you’d rather it didn’t look.
  • If nothing can be downloaded, boundaries saved from an earlier release are returned with a warning.

In each of those cases a warning says what you were given.
